column3: A database lists Panthera leo and Panthera tigris under the same genus, while a lichen specimen consists of a fungal partner associated with a photosynthetic partner. Which conclusion follows without confusing naming rank with the number of biological partners?
column4: The two Panthera names denote one species because the first word is shared
column5: A lichen must be assigned to Panthera because it contains more than one cell type
column6: The specific epithets alone establish that leo and tigris belong to different kingdoms
column7: The two animals share a genus but are different named species; the lichen's association is not itself a taxonomic rank equivalent to genus
column9:
Answer: (D) A shared generic name and a symbiotic association describe different kinds of organisation.
Why: In binomial nomenclature the first word identifies the genus and the second contributes the specific epithet. The two listed animals therefore share Panthera but have different complete species names. A lichen is an association of fungal and photosynthetic partners, not a new rank in the genus–species hierarchy. Its composite organisation cannot be inferred from, or used to redefine, the naming rules for the animals.
Why not the others: (A) treats sharing a genus as identity of species. (B) invents a relation between a lichen association and an animal genus. (C) tries to infer a kingdom distinction from specific epithets despite the common genus.
Key point: Keep the rank encoded by a scientific name separate from the ecological relationship among organisms.
column10: Shared binomial genus and a lichen association describe different classification and ecological relations
column11: The living world: taxonomic categories and nomenclature; biological classification: lichens

column3: The root-modification diagram shows P growing upward from waterlogged soil, Q descending from spreading branches into soil, and R arising from lower stem nodes obliquely into the soil. Which assignment of their principal functions is correct?
column4: P mechanical support only; Q respiration only; R food storage
column5: P gaseous exchange; Q prop-root support; R stilt-root support
column6: P mineral-free photosynthesis; Q pollination; R seed dispersal
column7: P absorption of atmospheric nitrogen gas; Q storage cotyledons; R tendrils
column9:
Answer: (B) The upward respiratory roots differ from two mechanically supportive root arrangements.
Why: Waterlogged soil restricts gaseous exchange, and pneumatophores projecting above it provide an aerating route. Prop roots descend from branches and can support a broad crown, as in banyan. Stilt roots arise from lower stem nodes and enter the soil obliquely, as in maize or sugarcane. Their position of origin and direction are therefore relevant to function; a root projecting upward is not simply another support column.
Why not the others: (A) exchanges the gas-exchange role of P with Q's supporting geometry. (C) attributes reproductive or photosynthetic functions not supported by these root forms. (D) confuses gas exchange with direct nitrogen-gas assimilation and labels roots as cotyledons or tendrils.
Key point: Infer root modification from its origin, orientation and environmental constraint together.
column10: Respiratory, prop and stilt roots distinguished by origin and environmental function
column11: Morphology of flowering plants: root modifications

column3: A membrane protein has tags N and C. In native cells N faces the extracellular fluid and C faces the cytosol. Two preparations form sealed vesicles. External protease removes N but not C in P, and C but not N in Q. Detergent added before protease makes both tags disappear in both preparations. Protease cannot cross an intact bilayer and the tags are detected independently. Which inference uses all controls?
column4: P retains native outside-out orientation and Q is inside-out; detergent results show that prior protection reflected inaccessibility rather than intrinsic protease resistance
column5: P and Q both have native orientation; loss of different tags proves that the two proteins have different amino-acid sequences
column6: Q must be freely permeable to protease, because one tag is lost; the protected tag can be ignored
column7: Protease resistance of the protected tag is established permanently, so detergent must destroy the tag chemically without protease
column9:
Answer: (A) The two sealed preparations expose opposite native faces, and detergent removes the access barrier.
Why: P exposes N, the region facing extracellular fluid in the native cell, while protecting the cytosolic C tag. That is the native outside-out arrangement. Q instead exposes C and protects N, which fits an inside-out orientation rather than complete membrane leakage. In each preparation the previously protected tag becomes protease-sensitive after detergent disrupts the bilayer. That control separates a physical accessibility difference from an intrinsically uncleavable tag. Independent tag detection prevents disappearance of one signal from being mistaken for loss of the entire protein.
Why not the others: (B) ignores the known native topology and invents sequence differences that are unnecessary to explain the opposite access. (C) predicts access to both tags if the membrane were freely permeable, contrary to the retained protected tag. (D) contradicts the detergent-plus-protease result by treating a reversible access restriction as permanent chemical resistance.
Key point: Combine sidedness, impermeability and a barrier-removal control before inferring membrane-protein orientation.
column10: Protease access and detergent rescue distinguish opposite vesicle orientations from protein resistance or membrane leakage
column11: Cell the unit of life: plasma membrane; lipid bilayer; integral proteins; membrane asymmetry

column3: In an actively respiring mitochondrion, an enzyme converts succinate to fumarate and transfers electrons into the respiratory chain. Most other citric-acid-cycle enzymes are in the matrix. Which combination correctly identifies the exceptional enzyme location and distinguishes its role from substrate-level phosphorylation?
column4: Succinate dehydrogenase is a soluble cytosolic enzyme that directly makes all mitochondrial ATP
column5: Succinate dehydrogenase is in the outer membrane and directly synthesises GTP from succinate
column6: Succinate dehydrogenase is associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane; substrate-level GTP formation occurs at the succinyl-CoA-to-succinate step instead
column7: The citric acid cycle occurs entirely in the intermembrane space and contains no substrate-level phosphorylation
column9:
Answer: (C) Succinate oxidation is membrane linked, whereas a different cycle step yields substrate-level GTP.
Why: Succinate dehydrogenase participates in the citric acid cycle and in electron transfer associated with the inner mitochondrial membrane. It is the location exception to the mainly matrix-localised cycle enzymes. The conversion of succinyl-CoA to succinate instead couples a high-energy substrate transformation to nucleotide phosphorylation. Electron delivery to the respiratory chain and direct substrate-level phosphorylation are distinct contributions to respiration, even though both occur within the overall mitochondrial pathway.
Why not the others: (A) gives the enzyme the wrong compartment and treats one step as the source of all ATP. (B) places it in the wrong membrane and confuses it with the GTP-forming step. (D) relocates the whole cycle and denies a retained phosphorylation reaction.
Key point: Locate individual respiratory reactions and distinguish electron transfer from direct nucleotide phosphorylation.
column10: Membrane-associated succinate dehydrogenase distinguished from the separate substrate-level GTP step
column11: Respiration in plants: tricarboxylic acid cycle; respiratory electron transport

column3: After axons connecting the hypothalamus to the posterior pituitary are cut, posterior-pituitary hormone release is greatly reduced. Which statement correctly distinguishes the normal sites of synthesis and storage/release?
column4: Oxytocin and vasopressin are normally synthesised by posterior-pituitary epithelial cells
column5: These hormones are synthesised in hypothalamic neurons and transported to the posterior pituitary for storage and release
column6: The anterior pituitary normally synthesises both hormones and sends them through the cut axons
column7: The cut must stop thyroid follicular cells from synthesising thyroxine directly
column9:
Answer: (B) Hypothalamic synthesis is separated from posterior-pituitary storage and release.
Why: Oxytocin and vasopressin are produced by hypothalamic neurosecretory neurons. Their axons carry the hormones to endings associated with the posterior pituitary, where they are stored and released into the circulation. Cutting this connection therefore disrupts the delivery/release arrangement without making the posterior pituitary the original synthesis site. The result concerns this neural pathway rather than every endocrine gland.
Why not the others: (A) assigns synthesis to the storage/release region instead of hypothalamic neurons. (C) substitutes the anterior pituitary for the neuronal source. (D) claims a direct block in a separate gland without evidence connecting it to the severed axons.
Key point: The organ releasing a hormone need not be the tissue that synthesised it.
column10: Hypothalamic synthesis distinguished from posterior-pituitary storage and release
column11: Chemical coordination and integration: hypothalamus; pituitary hormones

column3: A primary oocyte is arrested in prophase I before birth. Near ovulation it completes meiosis I unequally, and the secondary oocyte arrests again until fertilisation. Which sequence correctly states the later arrest and the reason only one large functional female gamete is normally produced?
column4: Metaphase I arrest; all cytoplasm is shared equally among four eggs
column5: Prophase II arrest; DNA replication between meiotic divisions doubles egg number
column6: Anaphase I arrest; polar bodies become equally large ova
column7: Metaphase II arrest; unequal cytokinesis retains most cytoplasm in one cell, and meiosis II completes after sperm entry
column9:
Answer: (D) The ovulated secondary oocyte is normally arrested at metaphase II and retains most cytoplasm.
Why: Completion of meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes while dividing the cytoplasm unequally. The secondary oocyte keeps most of that cytoplasm, whereas a small polar body receives the other chromosome set. It enters meiosis II and arrests at metaphase II; sperm entry triggers completion. This arrangement preserves cellular resources in one prospective ovum rather than distributing them among four equally large functional eggs.
Why not the others: (A) names the wrong arrest and replaces unequal cytokinesis with equal division. (B) invents replication between the two meiotic divisions and gives the wrong phase. (C) places the arrest during chromosome separation and wrongly promotes polar bodies into equivalent ova.
Key point: Follow meiotic stage and cytoplasmic allocation separately in oogenesis.
column10: Oocyte arrest timing and unequal cytoplasmic allocation explain one large functional gamete
column11: Human reproduction: oogenesis; fertilisation and completion of meiosis II

column3: An RNA molecule in a laboratory reaction catalyses cleavage of another RNA, and its sequence is itself copied when the necessary machinery is supplied. Which inference is consistent with the RNA-world argument without exceeding this evidence?
column4: RNA can combine informational and catalytic roles; the result does not imply that every modern organism has an RNA genome
column5: RNA catalysis proves that DNA cannot store hereditary information
column6: A catalytic RNA must be a protein because all biological catalysts contain amino-acid chains
column7: The reaction establishes the complete historical sequence of the origin of the first cell
column9:
Answer: (A) The demonstrated dual capabilities support a possible early role for RNA without establishing a universal modern genome or complete history.
Why: An RNA sequence can encode information, and some RNA molecules also catalyse reactions. Combining these properties makes RNA a plausible participant in early systems before the modern division of labour among DNA, RNA and proteins. The experiment demonstrates capabilities under supplied conditions, not the genome type of every present-day organism. It also does not reconstruct all steps by which autonomous living systems originated.
Why not the others: (B) denies DNA's established informational role without a relevant test. (C) mistakes the chemical nature of a ribozyme for a polypeptide enzyme. (D) turns a limited molecular observation into proof of an entire historical pathway.
Key point: Distinguish evidence for a molecule's possible evolutionary role from proof of a complete origin scenario.
column10: RNA information and catalysis support an RNA-world possibility without a universal modern-genome claim
column11: Molecular basis of inheritance: RNA world; catalytic RNA

column3: A matched assay compares ingestion by phagocytes and blockade of microbial entry into target cells. Naive phagocytes ingest microbes A and B equally well. Serum from an A-immunised donor blocks entry of A but not B without phagocytes. Removing antibodies from that serum abolishes entry blockade; adding the isolated antibodies back restores it. Washed phagocytes from the immunised donor, tested without serum, ingest A and B at the same rates as naive phagocytes. Which conclusion and prediction are supported?
column4: Prior immunisation has made the phagocytes specifically recognise only A; antibody removal should abolish all phagocytic ingestion
column5: All observed protection is innate because a phagocyte can ingest either microbe; the serum-specific result is irrelevant
column6: Broad phagocyte ingestion and A-specific antibody blockade are separable defences; removing antibodies need not remove ingestion, and these results do not establish antigen-specific memory in the washed phagocytes
column7: The serum acts as an intact physical skin barrier; isolated antibodies cannot be responsible because no phagocytes are present
column9:
Answer: (C) The data separate a broad cellular innate function from a specific antibody-mediated acquired function.
Why: Naive and donor phagocytes show the same ingestion of A and B, so these measurements do not demonstrate an A-specific change in the washed phagocytes. By contrast, the donor serum blocks only A, and loss after antibody removal followed by rescue on add-back ties that measured blockade to antibodies. The two assays measure different processes, ingestion and entry inhibition; removing one mechanism therefore need not abolish the other. Prior immunisation is relevant to the antibody specificity, but it does not justify assigning every donor-cell effect to memory.
Why not the others: (A) contradicts equal A/B ingestion and extends antibody depletion to an independently measured cellular function. (B) ignores the antigen-specific serum effect and its removal/rescue controls. (D) confuses a soluble molecular defence with skin and denies the demonstrated antibody rescue.
Key point: Use selective removal and rescue in matched assays to distinguish coexisting innate and acquired mechanisms.
column10: Antibody removal and add-back distinguish specific serum blockade from unchanged broad phagocyte ingestion
column11: Human health and disease: innate cellular barriers; acquired humoral immunity; antibodies and specificity

column3: DNA is to be isolated from bacterial, plant and fungal cells. After appropriate cell-wall treatment, all lysates contain DNA, RNA and protein. Which protocol matches the wall differences while preserving DNA?
column4: Use cellulase for bacteria, lysozyme for fungi, then DNase to purify DNA
column5: Use lysozyme for bacteria, cellulase for plant material and chitinase for fungi; remove RNA with RNase and protein with protease before precipitating DNA
column6: Use chitinase for plants and RNase to remove all nucleic acids except protein
column7: Add DNase before wall disruption because precipitation will reconstruct the hydrolysed DNA
column9:
Answer: (B) Wall-specific enzymes are followed by selective removal of contaminating RNA and protein.
Why: Bacterial, plant and fungal walls have different major structural materials, so lysozyme, cellulase and chitinase are appropriate respective choices in the standard isolation context. Once cells are lysed, RNase degrades RNA and protease removes proteins while DNA is retained. Chilled ethanol can then precipitate DNA from the prepared material. A precipitation step separates molecules; it cannot reverse nuclease hydrolysis of the desired DNA.
Why not the others: (A) mismatches walls and destroys the target with DNase. (C) assigns a fungal-wall enzyme to plant cellulose and confuses RNA removal with elimination of every nucleic acid. (D) intentionally hydrolyses the target and assumes precipitation repairs it.
Key point: Match the lysis enzyme to the wall and the cleanup enzyme to the contaminant, preserving the molecule sought.
column10: Wall-specific lysis and selective nuclease cleanup distinguish DNA isolation from target destruction
column11: Biotechnology principles and processes: isolation of genetic material

column3: A threatened wild plant is protected in its native forest, and seeds from several populations are also stored in a seed bank. Which interpretation correctly classifies these conservation actions?
column4: Forest protection and seed banking are both in situ because both involve the same species
column5: Seed banking alone preserves every ecological interaction of the native forest
column6: Forest protection is ex situ because humans designate the protected area
column7: Forest protection is in situ; seed banking is ex situ and preserves genetic material without recreating the entire native ecosystem
column9:
Answer: (D) Protecting the natural population differs from storing resources outside its habitat.
Why: In situ conservation maintains organisms within their natural ecological setting, where interactions and environmental processes can continue. A seed bank holds material outside that setting and is therefore an ex situ measure. Sampling several populations can retain more genetic representation, but storage does not reproduce pollination, competition and other forest interactions. The two approaches can complement one another without being ecologically identical.
Why not the others: (A) classifies by species identity instead of conservation setting. (B) attributes a complete ecosystem to stored seeds. (C) confuses human management with the location of conservation relative to the native habitat.
Key point: Distinguish where conservation occurs from the identity of the species being conserved.
column10: Native-population protection and seed banking conserve different levels of biological context
column11: Biodiversity and conservation: in situ and ex situ conservation

column3: A true-breeding red-flowered plant is crossed with a true-breeding white-flowered plant. F1 flowers are pink, and F1 selfing produces approximately one red:two pink:one white. Under a single-locus model, which conclusion separates allele segregation from the claim of complete dominance?
column4: The alleles segregate normally, but the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype rather than the phenotype of either homozygote
column5: The 1:2:1 ratio proves that alleles blend and cannot separate again
column6: Segregation is absent because the phenotype ratio is not 3:1
column7: The F1 must contain only one allele because it has one visible colour
column9:
Answer: (A) Incomplete dominance changes genotype-to-phenotype mapping without abolishing segregation.
Why: The F1 heterozygote transmits either parental allele, and selfing yields the familiar homozygote:heterozygote:homozygote genotype ratio of 1:2:1. When the heterozygote is phenotypically distinct, that genotype ratio is visible directly as three flower-colour classes. A 3:1 phenotype ratio requires one allele to mask the other completely, which is not the observation here. Recovery of both parental colours in F2 is inconsistent with irreversible blending.
Why not the others: (B) ignores the reappearance of the parental phenotypes. (C) treats complete dominance as a requirement for segregation. (D) confuses one observed colour with one copy of a gene in a diploid cell.
Key point: Test allele transmission separately from how heterozygotes express the transmitted alleles.
column10: Incomplete dominance alters phenotype classes without invalidating Mendelian allele segregation
column11: Principles of inheritance and variation: incomplete dominance; segregation

column3: Two skeletal muscle preparations have equal initial force. P has abundant myoglobin, mitochondria and capillaries; Q has much less of these. During prolonged repeated stimulation with adequate oxygen delivery, then during a brief interruption of oxygen supply, which comparison is most defensible?
column4: Q must resist prolonged fatigue better because fewer mitochondria require less oxygen
column5: P cannot use oxygen because myoglobin permanently traps it
column6: P is better equipped for sustained oxidative activity; Q relies relatively more on anaerobic metabolism, and interruption of oxygen removes P's aerobic advantage without proving instant reversal of every performance measure
column7: Both have identical fatigue behaviour because equal initial force determines endurance
column9:
Answer: (C) The structural evidence predicts different metabolic capacities rather than a universal force ranking.
Why: Myoglobin supports oxygen availability within muscle, and abundant mitochondria and capillaries favour sustained aerobic ATP production in red fibres. White fibres rely relatively more on anaerobic routes and tend to fatigue sooner during prolonged activity under suitable oxygen supply. Removing that supply limits the oxidative route, so P's advantage cannot simply be assumed to persist unchanged. Equal initial force does not establish equal energy reserves, metabolic capacity or later endurance.
Why not the others: (A) treats limited oxidative machinery as an endurance advantage under adequate oxygen. (B) denies reversible oxygen binding and release by myoglobin. (D) infers the entire fatigue time course from one initial mechanical measurement.
Key point: Link fibre structure to ATP-supply capacity while stating the oxygen conditions of the comparison.
column10: Red and white fibre structure predicts oxygen-dependent endurance rather than an unconditional force ranking
column11: Locomotion and movement: skeletal muscle; red and white muscle fibres

column3: In a dialysis model, blood and fresh dialysing fluid are separated by a membrane permeable to urea, water and small ions but impermeable to blood cells and large plasma proteins. The fluid has the same useful small-ion concentrations as blood but no urea. Pressure is balanced, and active transport is absent. Which initial net changes are expected?
column4: Plasma proteins leave rapidly because their concentration is high, while urea stays in blood
column5: Blood cells cross until cell numbers on both sides become equal
column6: Every small ion necessarily leaves blood at the same net rate as urea
column7: Urea diffuses into the fluid; useful ions have little initial net diffusion under the matched concentrations, and cells and large proteins remain in blood
column9:
Answer: (D) Net movement requires both membrane permeability and an appropriate gradient.
Why: Urea has a concentration difference directed from blood to initially urea-free dialysing fluid and can cross the model membrane. Matching useful small-ion concentrations avoids a comparable initial net diffusive loss of those ions. Blood cells and large plasma proteins cannot cross despite their concentration differences because the membrane excludes them. Balanced pressure also removes an imposed bulk-filtration explanation for the selective initial solute movement.
Why not the others: (A) ignores the protein permeability restriction and reverses urea movement. (B) makes an impermeant cellular component behave like a diffusible solute. (C) treats permeability alone as sufficient for a net flux, ignoring the matched ionic concentrations.
Key point: Predict dialysis from gradients and membrane selectivity together, not from concentration or molecular size alone.
column10: Dialysis separates urea removal from useful-ion retention through both gradients and permeability
column11: Excretory products and their elimination: kidney failure; haemodialysis

column3: A very short DNA-label pulse marks cells currently in S phase. In a model culture every cell has the same fixed phase durations, all are cycling, and cells at every point of S phase are represented. The first labelled cells enter mitosis 2 h after the pulse and the last labelled cells enter mitosis 7 h after it. M lasts 1 h and the full cycle 12 h. Neglect pulse duration. What are S and G1 durations?
column9:
Answer: (B) S lasts 5 h and G1 lasts 4 h.
Given: The labelled cohort initially spans the entire S phase; G2 and M durations are fixed.
Formula/Principle: The earliest labelled mitoses come from cells at the end of S, whereas the latest come from cells at its beginning.
Step 1: The first entry gives \[T_{G2}=2\ \mathrm{h}.\]
Step 2: The spread of entry times gives \[T_S=7-2=5\ \mathrm{h}.\]
Step 3: Subtract known phases from the cycle: \[T_{G1}=12-(5+2+1)=4\ \mathrm{h}.\]
Why: The labelled cells have different amounts of S remaining but the same G2 still ahead. The entry-time difference therefore isolates S rather than the whole interval from pulse to the last mitosis.
Why not the others: (A) includes G2 in S. (C) exchanges G2 with S. (D) omits G2 from the full-cycle subtraction.
Key point: Use the leading and trailing edges of a pulse-labelled cohort to separate consecutive phase durations.
column10: Edges of a pulse-labelled mitotic cohort distinguish S duration from the following G2 delay
column11: Cell cycle and cell division: interphase; S and G2 phases; mitosis

column3: After delivery, a mother's mammary glands synthesise milk, but a temporary inhibition of oxytocin release prevents effective ejection during suckling. Which interpretation separates milk production from its delivery?
column4: Prolactin and oxytocin are interchangeable names for the same hormone
column5: Loss of oxytocin proves that no milk can have been synthesised
column6: Prolactin supports milk production, while oxytocin normally promotes contraction of myoepithelial cells for milk ejection
column7: Milk ejection is caused by inhibition of all mammary muscle contraction
column9:
Answer: (C) Milk synthesis and milk ejection depend on different hormone-linked processes.
Why: Prolactin promotes milk production in the mammary glands. Oxytocin released during the suckling response promotes contraction of myoepithelial cells, which helps move the milk into the ducts for ejection. Inhibiting the second process can therefore impair delivery even when milk has already been made. An observed failure of ejection is not by itself evidence that the synthetic process failed.
Why not the others: (A) collapses distinct hormones and actions into one. (B) infers absent synthesis from a downstream delivery defect. (D) reverses the mechanical role of contraction in ejection.
Key point: Distinguish production of a biological material from the regulated mechanism that releases it.
column10: Prolactin-supported milk synthesis distinguished from oxytocin-driven myoepithelial ejection
column11: Human reproduction: lactation; chemical coordination: prolactin and oxytocin
